title: Why You Should Never Argue With Students; And How To Avoid It and-how-to-avoid-it/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Opening with a scenario of a student denying obvious misbehavior in a hallway line, Linsin explains why teachers should never let themselves be drawn into arguments with students. He lists the costs of arguing — stress, lost composure, wasted time, weakened relationships, and an implicit invitation for students to challenge authority — and notes that some students provoke arguments precisely because it puts them on equal footing with the teacher. He then lays out a five-step method for avoiding arguments altogether: follow the classroom management plan instead of merely asking students to stop, give a warning, disengage and move on, pause and repeat the warning if a student persists, and escalate to a second consequence if the arguing continues. The piece frames this approach as both protecting classroom momentum and ultimately strengthening a teacher's credibility, since there is nothing left to prove once a consistent plan is simply followed.
points: Arguing with students wastes instructional time and erodes the teacher-student relationship, even when the teacher is 'right.'
Some students provoke arguments deliberately because disagreement puts them on the same level as the teacher.
Following a classroom management plan — warning, then consequence — removes the need to argue at all.
After a warning, the teacher should disengage immediately rather than give the student room to plead a case.
If arguing continues, it becomes its own rule violation deserving its own consequence.
quotes: But while you’re battling it out with Andrew, your students are waiting and growing bored, your upcoming lesson is on hold, and the smooth momentum of your day is lost.
Some students will try to goad you into an argument because it puts you on the same level. In other words, it becomes just two people disagreeing.

1. Follow Your Classroom Management Plan – Arguments begin when the teacher asks a student to stop doing something rather than enforcing a consequence. Your classroom rules should cover every possible misbehavior.

After giving a warning, or a time-out if it’s a second offense, turn away from the student immediately and continue with whatever you were doing. Don’t give your students an opportunity to argue or explain their behavior.

If you find yourself in a situation where a student is determined to stand in front of you to plead his or her case, maintain eye contact, pause several seconds, and then repeat, “You have a warning because you are not keeping your hands to yourself.
And the best part is you’ll never again have to prove to your students what you—and they—already know to be the truth.
